summary: Most probable root cause: the 12:00 UTC config change that raised HOLDINGS_CACHE_TTL_S on portfolio-svc from 60 s to 1800 s. Cache staleness was 0 through 11:59, rose from 12:00, reached the 1800 s ceiling by about 12:09, and stayed there. Logs show holdings served from cache with entry ages climbing to 1800 s. The write path looks healthy: the queue is not backing up, there are no dead letters, error rates are low, and postgres is fine. The 'had no changes' consumer WARNs and the upstream aa-sync feed are not established as causes. The link to the config change rests on timing and log correlation, not on a direct check of applied TTLs.

hypotheses.statement: The 12:00 UTC change that raised HOLDINGS_CACHE_TTL_S on portfolio-svc from 60 s to 1800 s lets the holdings cache serve entries for up to 30 minutes, so balance reads omit trades older than ten minutes even though the write path works.
hypotheses.label: high

supporting.text: The config change at 12:00:00Z raised HOLDINGS_CACHE_TTL_S from 60 s to 1800 s, and it is the only recorded change on portfolio-svc in the window.
Staleness was 0 up to 11:59, began rising at 12:00, and reached 1800 s by 12:09. It stayed at the ceiling through the end of the window, which matches the new TTL value.

Logs show holdings served from cache with entry ages stepping up to 1800 s by 12:09:18, still 1800 s at 12:59:50. This is consistent with entries living up to 30 minutes, so trades older than ten minutes would be missing.

portfolio-svc is directly on the balance read path (called by web-app and orchestrator, calling redis-cache). Redis evictions were zero, so cache pressure or an INC-0412-style eviction does not explain the staleness.
It is likely that the steady ramp of about 180 s per minute reflects no holdings refresh after 12:00. This is an inference from the shape of the series.

contradicting.text: The first logged cache-serve line at 12:00:22 shows an entry age of 180 s, longer than the old 60 s TTL. If so, the new TTL may have taken effect before the logged change time, or the record time is off. This ordering is unreconciled.

The staleness metric jumps to 540 s or 180 s at 12:00 (the two series disagree), while log entry ages climb gradually. The metric and the logs may measure different things, so they are not fully reconciled.

hypotheses.statement: portfolio-consumer treats some portfolio-updates messages as 'no changes' and skips them, so real trade changes never reach postgres and balances stay stale at the source.
hypotheses.label: low

supporting.text: portfolio-consumer logged 20 'update N had no changes' WARNs from 11:17:47 to 12:56:51. For update 583 there is a no-changes WARN but no 'processed' line, while a different update was logged as processed.

contradicting.text: Consumer error rate was low and throughput steady at about 40 rps. Postgres showed no pool saturation and low write latency. Redeliveries were low. Only about 20 WARNs appeared against roughly 40 messages per second, so this is a tiny fraction of traffic.
Staleness was 0 at 11:59, after the first no-changes WARN at 11:17. If dropped updates were the cause, staleness would already have been elevated before 12:00.
Whether the dropped updates carried real trades is unverified. Payloads were not available, so the idea that a real trade was discarded remains an assumption.

hypotheses.statement: aa-sync, the only listed producer of portfolio-updates, publishes stale or incomplete trade data, or trades from broker-gateway and order-router never reach it, so a healthy downstream pipeline is fed old data.
hypotheses.label: low

supporting.text: aa-sync is the only listed producer of portfolio-updates, so stale or incomplete data from it would propagate downstream. The graph shows no trade path from broker-gateway or order-router into the queue.

contradicting.text: Publish and consume rates are close and steady, so the feed is flowing and the queue is not backing up.
No aa-sync or order-router change was recorded in the window. This is limited to recorded changes only.

facts.text: portfolio-svc cache_staleness_s over 11:00-13:00 peaked at 1800 s, with the last sample also at 1800 s and a mean of 832.5 s.
portfolio-consumer error rate stayed low (min 0.002, max 0.004, last 0.004).
First portfolio-consumer WARN in the window: an update was reported as having no changes, and these WARNs recur through 12:56:51Z (20 lines total, no ERROR lines returned).
Publish rate and consume rate were close, with consume rate slightly higher on average, so the queue was not backing up.
Redeliveries were low but non-zero, with a mean of 0.272 and a max of 0.375.
portfolio-consumer error rate was low (mean 0.003, max 0.004), and its throughput was steady at about 40 rps.
Postgres showed no connection pool saturation and write latency near 8 ms, which does not support a DB bottleneck.
portfolio-svc config change raised the holdings cache TTL from 60 s to 1800 s, 30 minutes before the report and closest to onset.
portfolio-svc calls redis-cache (weight 0.2) and postgres (weight 0.8), and is called by orchestrator and web-app, so a cache TTL change there sits directly on the balance read path.
portfolio-updates has aa-sync as its only listed producer.
Staleness first became non-zero at the 12:00 sample, at 540 s, which is below 600 s. The earliest deviation is bracketed between 11:55 and 12:00.
Portfolio-svc served holdings from cache with entry age 180s at 12:00:22, the first cache-serve line in the window. Entry ages then increase in steps to 1800 s.
Entry age reached the 1800 s TTL ceiling in the logs by 12:09:18 and was still 1800 s in the last cache-serve line, at 12:59:50.
Redis evicted_keys was zero throughout the window, so there is no eviction signal. This weakens the INC-0412-style Redis-eviction hypothesis for this incident.
In the 11:17 minute, portfolio-consumer logged a 'processed' line for a different update (757632) at 11:17:08Z, but no 'processed' line for update 583, only the no-changes WARN at 11:17:47Z.
portfolio-updates has aa-sync as its only publisher and portfolio-consumer as its only consumer.
The change query for 11:00-13:00 UTC returned four records with no truncation, so no aa-sync or order-router change appears in the window.
Staleness was 0.0 at 11:17, inside the 11:03-11:17 window the task asked about, so it was not elevated there.
Staleness was 0.0 at the start of the window (11:00) and at 11:59, the minute before the rise.
Staleness rose from 0 to 180 s at the first minute after 12:00, the start of the increase.
Staleness reached the 1800 s ceiling at 12:09 and stayed there for the rest of the window.
portfolio-svc has a config change at 12:00:00Z that changes the holdings cache TTL from 60 to 1800 seconds.
The portfolio-svc config change record has no source or URL attached, and it is the only change returned for portfolio-svc in the 11:00-13:00 window across deploy, config, migration and flag kinds.

assumptions.text: An entry age of 180 s at 12:00:22 is longer than the pre-change 60 s TTL. The entry was filled around 11:57 (after the 11:57:28 miss), so the new TTL may have applied before the logged 12:00 change, or the config record time is off. This ordering is suspicious and unverified.

Staleness jumps from 0 at 11:55 to 540 at 12:00, while logged entry ages climb gradually from 180 s. The metric and the logs may measure different quantities (for example, max staleness versus sampled entry age), so they are not directly reconciled.
The 'had no changes' path probably skips the postgres write, so the update may not have changed holdings. This is inferred from the log wording and the missing write line and is not verified.

Because update 583 has no processed line and no postgres write, the consumer may have discarded a real trade rather than applying it. This is unverified and needs payload contents and the affected account's holdings rows.

The steady +180 s per minute ramp from 12:00 to 12:09 looks like staleness growing with wall-clock time since the last holdings refresh, which means no refresh happened after 12:00. This is inferred from the shape of the series and is not confirmed by any log.

actions.text: Revert HOLDINGS_CACHE_TTL_S on portfolio-svc from 1800 s to 60 s (change cfg-holdings-cache-ttl), and confirm all instances reload it.
actions.rationale: The TTL change matches the onset and the staleness plateau at the new TTL, and it is the only recorded portfolio-svc change. Reverting stops stale balances from being served.

actions.text: After the revert, purge or expire the existing holdings keys in redis-cache, or let them age out, so that entries written under the 1800 s TTL are not still served.
actions.rationale: It is likely that keys written after 12:00 carry the long TTL and will persist for up to 30 minutes after a revert. This is an assumption, not checked in Redis.

actions.text: Watch cache_staleness_s on portfolio-svc after the revert and confirm it falls back to near 0, which would confirm the cause.
actions.rationale: Staleness was 0 before 12:00, so recovery to baseline would validate the TTL hypothesis.

actions.text: Add cache invalidation or refresh on trade events for holdings, or require review and a staleness check for changes to cache TTLs. The change record had no source or URL attached.
actions.rationale: A long TTL with no invalidation on writes lets stale balances be served. The record lacked provenance, and whether trades trigger invalidation was not verified.

actions.rationale: This is a separate anomaly that is not established as harmful. Payloads were not logged, so it cannot be ruled out or confirmed from the available evidence.

actions.text: Check trade timestamps in broker-gateway, order-router and aa-sync against portfolio-updates publish times, and clarify how trades reach aa-sync.
